strapline: Thirty ministries approved and two old hands return, the cost argument, cholera stops a train, and a Lima MP walks out on bail

stories.title: Thirty ministries and two familiar faces: Parliament approves Hichilema's realignment a day after it was tabled, as Felix Mutati and Douglas Syakalima are nominated and sworn in
stories.excerpt: The National Assembly adopted the Vice-President's motion on Tuesday 27 October, clearing the way for a government of 30 ministries built around separate portfolios for Electricity, Petroleum, Trade and Exports, Industry, Housing and Skills and Higher Education. News Diggers reports that the President has nominated two former ministers to Parliament and that the Speaker swore them in. The published documents carry no cost estimate, and whether Friday's budget presentation still stands was not confirmed.

image.label: Thirty ministries
image.caption: Parliament approved the establishment, merger and dissolution of ministries on Tuesday 27 October 2026, a day after the President's request was announced.

body: Parliament has approved President Hakainde Hichilema's reorganisation of government ministries. The Zambian Observer reported on Tuesday 27 October that the House had given the President "green light" for 30 ministries after a motion moved by Vice-President Mutale Nalumango, and News Diggers reported on Wednesday morning that the House adopted the motion after debate. The motion, moved under Article 92(2)(d) of the Constitution, sought approval for the establishment, merger and dissolution of government ministries and departments as proposed by the President. Neither report says whether the House divided or how many members voted each way.

The vote came a day after the request was made public. As Lusaka Brief reported on Tuesday, State House announced on Monday 26 October that the President had written to Parliament seeking the realignment, which it said would put the machinery of government behind the Grow Zambia Agenda. The Times of Zambia reported on Tuesday morning that the business order paper showed the Vice-President was expected to move the motion that day, and the Zambian Observer had reported on Monday evening that it was set for the 14:30 sitting.

Open Zambia published the appendix to the President's request on Tuesday. It lists 30 ministries: Trade and Exports; Industry; Small and Medium Enterprise Development; Agriculture; Fisheries and Livestock; Electricity; Petroleum; Transport and Logistics; Infrastructure and Urban Development; Housing; Lands; Defence; Home Affairs; Foreign Affairs; Finance and National Planning; Mines; Tourism; Water; Green Economy; Health; Information; Education; Skills and Higher Education; Technology and Science; Local Government; Justice; Labour; Community Development; Youth and Sports; and Culture and Arts.

The Zambian Observer's account of the documents, published on Monday, describes the main changes: the Ministry of Energy split into Electricity and Petroleum; Commerce, Trade and Industry divided so that Trade and Exports stands apart from Industry; Infrastructure, Housing and Urban Development reorganised into Infrastructure and Urban Development with a separate Ministry of Housing; Lands and Natural Resources becoming Lands; a new Ministry of Skills and Higher Education alongside Education; and Youth, Sport and Arts divided into Youth and Sports and a new Culture and Arts ministry. News Diggers names Energy, Infrastructure, Housing and Urban Development, Commerce, Trade and Industry, Lands and Natural Resources, and Youth, Sport and Arts among the ministries proposed for dissolution or realignment.

The outlets do not agree on the baseline. The Zambian Observer describes the change as an increase from 24 ministries to 30, a rise of six; News Diggers describes the motion as raising the number from 25 to 30. The Zambian Observer also noted on Monday that the documents before Parliament do not indicate what the additional ministries will cost to staff and run.

News Diggers reports that the President has nominated Felix Mutati, the former Minister of Technology and Science, and Douglas Syakalima, the former Minister of Education, and that the Speaker, Nelly Mutti, swore them in. The report does not say which portfolios, if any, they will hold, and no appointment to a ministry had been announced in any report read for this edition. Only four ministers have been appointed since the August election, as the Zambian Observer's analysis of the realignment notes and as Lusaka Brief has reported.

The Times of Zambia set out what the President did on taking office in 2021: he established the ministries of Green Economy and Environment, Small and Medium Enterprise Development, and Technology and Science; renamed seven others, including Finance to Finance and National Planning and Transport and Communications to Transport and Logistics; merged General Education and Higher Education into a single Ministry of Education; and moved Arts from Tourism to Youth and Sport. Several of those 2021 decisions are reversed by Tuesday's structure, which separates higher education and arts into ministries of their own.

The vote lands in budget week. News Diggers reported on Friday 24 October that the Vice-President's business statement set the presentation of the 2027 national budget by the Minister of Finance and National Planning, Situmbeko Musokotwane, for Friday 30 October, after which the Speaker would suspend House business for ten working days of sector analysis, with business resuming on 24 November. On Tuesday, Citizens First asked the President to postpone the presentation until a full Cabinet is in place, its spokesperson Stanley Mhango arguing, in a statement carried by the Zambian Observer, that ministers appointed days before the budget would be asked to defend a document they had no part in preparing. No report read for this edition confirmed whether the Friday date still stands.

body.confirmed: Parliament approved the motion on the establishment, merger and dissolution of ministries on Tuesday 27 October (Zambian Observer; News Diggers). The appendix lists 30 ministries (Open Zambia). News Diggers reports that Felix Mutati and Douglas Syakalima were nominated and sworn in by the Speaker. The business statement of 24 October set the budget for Friday 30 October (News Diggers).
body.unverified: The number of ministries before the change: 24 (Zambian Observer) or 25 (News Diggers). The vote count, if there was a division. Which portfolios Mutati and Syakalima will hold. The cost of the new ministries, which the published documents do not state. Whether the budget presentation has been moved from Friday 30 October: one outlet reported a new date on Tuesday, but that report could not be read for this edition and no other outlet carried it.

stories.title: 'I am surprised there is no Ministry of Ministers': the cost argument over 30 ministries, and the case made for Electricity, Petroleum, Housing and Culture
stories.excerpt: Chapter One Foundation asked Parliament to test whether the realignment is necessary and affordable, Brian Mushimba said Zambia needs consolidation rather than more bureaucracy, and Laura Miti asked how rural voters benefit. On the other side, Sunday Chanda argued that each new portfolio answers a real problem and Greyford Monde made the case for a dedicated electricity ministry.

image.label: Six more ministries
image.caption: The proposal to add six ministries drew calls for scrutiny from civil society and opposition figures, and detailed defences from supporters, on Tuesday 27 October 2026.

body: The realignment of ministries went through Parliament in a day, but the argument about it filled Tuesday. The Chapter One Foundation, in remarks by its executive director Josiah Kalala to Phoenix News and carried by the Zambian Observer, urged MPs to exercise independent judgment rather than simply approve the President's request. Reorganising ministries, Kalala argued, can be costly and disruptive, and merging them does not of itself make government more efficient; Parliament should test whether the changes are necessary, evidence-based, financially justified and in the public interest. In the same report Isaac Mwanza, described as a governance expert, welcomed the President's decision to seek parliamentary approval, describing the move as an attempt to activate the growth agenda, and noted that the Constitution fixes the number of ministries, which cannot be exceeded.

Brian Mushimba, president of the Organized People's Party, said the country needs consolidation rather than higher spending, and that government should deliver results with fewer layers of administration rather than adding ministries, offices and bureaucracy at the start of the Grow Zambia Agenda. "How do we make government more effective and less expensive without compromising service delivery?" he asked, in remarks carried by the Zambian Observer.

The activist Laura Miti questioned the priorities behind new ministries for Petroleum, Industry and Culture at a time when, she said, the Constituency Development Fund is reportedly facing cuts and the Food Reserve Agency cannot buy all the maize farmers offer. "I am surprised there is no Ministry of Ministers," she said, asking how the rural voters who returned the government to office would benefit. Citizens First, through its spokesperson Stanley Mhango, tied the structure to the budget: a budget prepared without line ministers, the party argued, raises questions of collective responsibility under Article 116 of the Constitution.

The fullest reply came from Sunday Chanda, in an open letter to Miti published by the Zambian Observer. On Petroleum, he argued that the ministry's job is fuel security, supply, storage and pricing, rather than finding oil, and that Zambia spends more than US$2 billion a year on fuel imports. On Housing, he said the existing infrastructure ministry has in practice meant roads and bridges while the housing deficit runs past two million units. On Industry, he argued the point is to process copper, soya and sugar inside Zambia rather than export them raw. On Culture, he said the sector had been starved of funding while sharing a ministry with football, and that events such as Kuomboka and Likumbi Lya Mize drive tourism. "Don't judge by names. Judge by the first 90 days," he wrote, while also saying Parliament should scrutinise the cost of 30 ministries.

Greyford Monde, in a statement published by the same outlet, made the case for a stand-alone Ministry of Electricity, citing a World Bank estimate that mining accounts for roughly half of Zambia's electricity consumption and pointing to countries with dedicated electricity ministries or mandates, among them Egypt, Ghana, India and South Africa, which appointed a minister responsible for electricity in 2023. "Zambia cannot build a modern industrial economy on an unreliable power supply," he said, arguing the ministry should be judged on outcomes such as round-the-clock household supply and reliable power for mines and industry.

The Zambian Observer's own analysis, written by Ollus Ndomu for The People's Brief, put the realignment alongside the enlarged Parliament, whose constituency seats rose from 156 to 226 with 40 proportional-representation seats added, and whose budget the piece puts at about K1.58 billion this year. It argued that the documents describe how responsibilities would be divided but do not show that the splits would work better, and recommended that Parliament demand a clear statement of the problems, the projected costs and the expected benefits before approving. The House approved the motion the same day.

stories.title: Leave PAYE alone, put 15 per cent into health, or do not present it at all: the asks pile up ahead of a 2027 budget scheduled for Friday
stories.excerpt: ZIPAR told a briefing on Monday that the government should not cut the PAYE rate because the Grow Zambia Agenda needs the revenue; the Resident Doctors Association wants health's share lifted from about 13 per cent to at least 15; and Citizens First wants the whole presentation held back until there is a Cabinet to defend it. The business statement of 24 October set the presentation for Friday 30 October.

image.label: Budget week
image.caption: Think-tank, doctors and an opposition party set out their demands as the 2027 budget presentation, scheduled for Friday 30 October 2026, approaches.

body: The Zambia Institute for Policy Analysis and Research does not want the Pay As You Earn rate reduced in the 2027 budget. Its executive director, Zali Chikuba, told a press briefing on Monday 26 October, reported by News Diggers, that the country needs more revenue to finance the Grow Zambia Agenda, and that a cut would work against that. Chikuba also said the institute expects more progress on TAZAMA open access, which it believes would improve efficiency and transparency in fuel supply, and he declined to treat the Ministry of Finance's two supplementary budgets in one year as evidence of poor planning, saying government sometimes lacks the information to plan ahead.

The Resident Doctors Association of Zambia has a different number in mind. Its president, Paul Chibwe, told News Diggers in an interview on Monday that the health sector should receive at least 15 per cent of the 2027 budget, up from about 13 per cent in 2026, so that more health workers can be recruited and posted to underserved areas. He said he expects an increase, particularly given the health agreement with the United States that is now in place.

Citizens First went further and asked for the presentation to be put off. Its spokesperson, Stanley Mhango, said in a statement carried by the Zambian Observer on Tuesday that the party understands the budget was prepared and concluded without input from line ministers, with no hearings, submissions or ministerial ownership in the process. Appointing a full Cabinet days before the presentation, he argued, would not let ministers take part in a process that is already closed, and they would be asked in Parliament to answer for decisions they had no part in making. "A budget without ministerial input raises authenticity concerns," he said, citing Article 116 of the Constitution on collective responsibility. The party acknowledged the budget may still pass, but said public buy-in and ownership of implementation matter.

Parliament's timetable, as reported by News Diggers on Friday 24 October, has the Minister of Finance and National Planning, Situmbeko Musokotwane, presenting the budget on Friday 30 October, with the House sitting from 14:15 until business concludes. The Speaker would then suspend House business for ten working days of sector analysis, resuming on 24 November alongside the Expanded Budget Committee. That timetable was published before Tuesday's approval of 30 ministries and the nomination of two former ministers to Parliament; no report read for this edition confirmed whether the Friday date still stands, and one report of a later date could not be verified.

stories.title: A 150 MW coal plant for Ndola and 245 MWp of solar for Mufulira and Kasama: the ERB clears 61 licences and permits worth K13.4 billion in proposed investment
stories.excerpt: The Energy Regulation Board's licensing committee met on 14 October and approved 48 licence applications, nine construction permits and four amendments to petroleum transport licences, covering about US$662.3 million of proposed spending across electricity, renewables and downstream petroleum, according to a statement reported by two energy trade outlets on Tuesday.

image.label: K13.4 billion
image.caption: The ERB licensing committee's decisions of 14 October 2026 cover a coal-fired plant in Ndola, solar plants in Mufulira and Kasama and petroleum facilities in three districts.

body: The Energy Regulation Board has approved 61 licensing decisions that it says carry about K13.4 billion, or US$662.3 million, in proposed investment. The approvals were made at a meeting of the board's licensing committee on 14 October and announced in a statement which SolarQuarter attributes to the ERB's public relations manager, Namokolo Kasumpa, dated 20 October. Both SolarQuarter and Green Building Africa reported the decisions on Tuesday 27 October. They comprise 48 initial and renewal licence applications, nine construction permit applications and four amendments to petroleum transportation licences.

Electricity takes the largest share, according to Green Building Africa, mainly because of capital-intensive generation projects. The named projects are a proposed 150 MW coal-fired thermal power plant in Ndola, a 125 MWp solar photovoltaic plant in Mufulira, the 120 MWp Kasama Solar PV Power Plant, and further solar developments at Chikuni and Rusangu in Monze, at Mwandi and at Chadiza. The approvals also cover an expansion of electricity distribution infrastructure in the Chambishi Multi-Facility Economic Zone in Kalulushi. Neither report gives a dollar split by subsector or the names of the developers.

On the downstream petroleum side, the committee approved proposed retail facilities in Chongwe, Ndola and Chibombo, and amendments that add tankers to existing transportation licences. The wider set of petroleum approvals covers transportation, distribution, importation, exportation, lubricant businesses and the retail of liquefied petroleum gas. Green Building Africa quotes the board as saying the LPG approvals support the transition to cleaner cooking. The renewable-energy approvals, it reports, are mainly for the manufacture, supply, installation and maintenance of generating equipment rather than for named sites.

The ERB describes its approach, in the words both outlets attribute to it, as facilitating responsible investment through transparent, efficient and predictable licensing processes, subject to compliance with legislation, regulatory requirements and safety standards. Neither report says over what period the K13.4 billion would be spent, nor whether any of the generation projects has reached financial close; an ERB licence or construction permit is a regulatory approval, not a confirmation that a project will be built.

The coal plant is the item likely to draw attention. The two reports describe it only as a proposed 150 MW coal-fired thermal plant in Ndola and give no developer, fuel source or timeline. The solar figures, by contrast, add to a pipeline the government has been promoting as it targets 10,000 MW of generation capacity, a figure Zambia's ambassador to Japan repeated in Tokyo on Monday, according to Zambia Monitor.

stories.title: 5,595 confiscated, 27 found: the Mpika North MP calls the Auditor-General's report a crime scene and demands an investigation into the missing Mukula logs
stories.excerpt: Francis Kapyanga says the government must account for 5,568 Mukula logs that the Mpika District Forestry Office recorded as confiscated between 2021 and 2025 but which a physical inspection in May 2026 could not find. The Auditor-General's 2025 report, which carries the finding, says the value of the missing logs could not be established.

image.label: 5,568 logs
image.caption: The Auditor-General's 2025 report found only 27 of 5,595 confiscated Mukula logs at the Mpika District Forestry Office in May 2026.

body: Francis Kapyanga, the NRPUP Member of Parliament for Mpika North, has demanded an investigation into the disappearance of 5,568 confiscated Mukula logs recorded in the Auditor-General's 2025 report. Speaking in an interview on Monday 26 October reported by News Diggers, he described the report as a crime scene and said it was unacceptable for valuable natural resources to go missing without anyone being held responsible. The logs, he said, could have raised revenue for the government if they had been properly disposed of.

The finding comes from a review of records at the Mpika District Forestry Office. According to the Zambian Observer's account of the report, published on 20 October and credited to Diamond TV, a status report from the office showed 5,595 Mukula logs confiscated between 2021 and 2025. A physical inspection in May 2026 found 27. The remaining 5,568 were unaccounted for, and their value could not be determined. The facilities fall under the Ministry of Green Economy and Environment. The report, as summarised by the Zambian Observer, carries no response from the ministry.

Zambia Monitor's summary of the report, published on 19 October, lists the Mukula finding alongside others: K3.56 billion in outstanding obligations in the health sector, some dating back to 2014; K626.64 million in uncollected penalties from mining licence holders and K30.48 million in outstanding annual area charges; US$433,820 collected for the Department of Immigration but not remitted to the Treasury; customs duties of K41.97 million and temporary imports worth K9.03 million that the Zambia Revenue Authority could not account for; 74,840 properties on which ground rent could not be assessed because of incomplete land records; irregularities of more than K72 million under the Farmer Input Support Programme; and 125 Ministry of Education officers paid K1.23 million in salaries who could not be accounted for.

The Acting Auditor-General, Patricia Malaila, is quoted by Zambia Monitor as saying that "the continued growth of these obligations places considerable pressure on public finances", and by the Zambian Observer as urging controlling officers to strengthen internal controls and ensure public resources are properly managed. Zambia Monitor reports her as saying the number of unresolved audit findings fell to 27 in 2025 from 33 in 2024.

Lusaka Brief has reported two of those findings this week: the deceased health workers kept on the payroll, on Monday, and the FISP irregularities, on Tuesday. Kapyanga's demand comes from the opposition benches in the province where the logs were seized, and it asks a question the report itself leaves open: not only where the logs went, but who was responsible for them between confiscation and the May inspection.

body.confirmed: The Auditor-General's 2025 report records 5,595 Mukula logs confiscated at the Mpika District Forestry Office between 2021 and 2025, of which 27 were found in a May 2026 inspection (Zambian Observer, citing Diamond TV; Zambia Monitor). Kapyanga called for an investigation on Monday (News Diggers).
body.unverified: What happened to the 5,568 logs, their value, and whether any officer is under investigation. No ministry response has been reported.

stories.title: A train held at Mapepe: 25 passengers on the Kitwe–Livingstone service taken to the Chilanga treatment centre, as the national count passes 1,480 cases and 29 deaths
stories.excerpt: Zambia Railways stopped passenger train 601 in the Chilanga area on Monday 26 October after a passenger fell ill with vomiting and diarrhoea; the Times of Zambia reports that 25 of about 500 people on board showed cholera symptoms and that 500 vaccine doses were brought to the train. ZNPHI's update the same day gave 68 new cases, one death and a cumulative 1,488 cases.

image.label: Train 601
image.caption: A southbound Zambia Railways passenger train was quarantined near Mapepe in Chilanga on Monday 26 October 2026 after suspected cholera cases on board.

body: A Zambia Railways passenger train bound for Livingstone was stopped in Chilanga on Monday 26 October after suspected cholera cases were found on board. In a written statement reported by News Diggers, the company's public relations manager, Sombe Longwani, said suspected cases had been reported aboard Passenger Train No. 601, travelling from Kitwe to Livingstone, and that the train was halted in the Chilanga area as a precaution while more than 20 passengers were taken to a health facility. The company said it is increasing surveillance on its passenger trains and working with health authorities to detect suspected cases earlier.

The Times of Zambia, whose crew was at the scene, reported that the southbound train was carrying about 500 passengers and was quarantined near Mapepe from about 07:00 after one passenger developed uncontrolled vomiting and diarrhoea. Railway officials reported the case and health authorities ordered the train not to proceed until medical staff had assessed it. By the paper's count, 25 passengers showed cholera symptoms and were moved to the Chilanga cholera treatment centre, where they were isolated and treated; the youngest was one year old and the oldest 80.

Kennedy Lishimpi, the Permanent Secretary for Technical Services at the Ministry of Health, told the Times of Zambia at the scene that the first case had boarded the train and fallen ill on it. "The initial case got onto the train, according to what we gathered in Kapiri Mposhi," he said. All the patients, including the first, were responding to treatment. Health authorities mobilised 500 doses of cholera vaccine so that every passenger could be vaccinated: "We have enough vaccines for them, and each person will be vaccinated," Lishimpi said. The Disaster Risk Management Division's national coordinator, Norman Chipakupaku, said the government provided food, water, tents and toilets for the stranded passengers.

body.text: We have enough vaccines for them, and each person will be vaccinated.
body.attribution: Kennedy Lishimpi, Permanent Secretary for Technical Services, Ministry of Health, speaking to the Times of Zambia at the Mapepe quarantine site on Monday 26 October

body: The Times of Zambia also carried the Zambia National Public Health Institute's figures for the same day: 68 new cases and one death, taking the cumulative count since the outbreak was declared to 1,488 cases and 29 deaths, with 103 patients admitted. That is 174 more cases and two more deaths than the ZNPHI tally of 1,314 cases and 27 deaths that Lusaka Brief reported on Tuesday, and it matches the higher figure of 1,488 cases and 29 deaths which that report noted but could not then match to a published ZNPHI bulletin; the Times of Zambia now attributes it to the institute's update of Monday 26 October. The two accounts of the train differ on the number affected, more than 20 in the Zambia Railways statement as reported by News Diggers, whose headline says 21, against 25 in the Times of Zambia, and the Times reports symptoms rather than laboratory confirmation in the body of its article.

stories.title: Out after eleven days: the High Court grants Lima MP Kelvin Kaunda K30,000 bail on an assault charge, the Zambian Observer reports, as he denies 'widespread violence' in court
stories.excerpt: Kaunda, the NRPUP member for the new Lima constituency, was arrested at the High Court on 15 October and held at Lubwa police post and then Mwembeshi Prison despite meeting police bond conditions. Judge Kaumbi Ndulo had ordered the State to produce him on Monday 27 October; the Zambian Observer reported that evening that bail was granted. He is also the respondent in an election petition in which he gave evidence on Monday.

image.label: Lima
image.caption: Kelvin Kaunda, the NRPUP MP for Lima, was arrested on 15 October 2026 on a charge of assault occasioning actual bodily harm and applied to the High Court for bail.

body: The Zambian Observer reported on Monday evening, 27 October, that the Lusaka High Court has granted bail to Kelvin Kaunda, the NRPUP Member of Parliament for Lima, after eleven days in detention. According to that report, bail was set at K30,000 with two working sureties in the same sum, bound by recognisance. No other outlet read for this edition had reported the decision by the time of publication.

The sequence that led to Monday's hearing is well documented. News Diggers reported on 24 October that Judge Kaumbi Ndulo had ordered the State to present Kaunda before him on 27 October for the hearing of his application for bail pending trial. Kaunda had been held since 15 October, when, as Zambia Monitor reported, he was arrested shortly after the High Court adjourned the hearing of a petition against his election. He is charged with assault occasioning actual bodily harm under section 248 of the Penal Code, over an alleged assault on a UPND supporter during a campaign roadshow on 7 August. He was first held at Lubwa police post and later moved to Mwembeshi Prison, a transfer confirmed to News Diggers by the Zambia Correctional Service's head of public relations, Superintendent Cornelius Mwanza.

In his affidavit, reported by Zambia Monitor on 21 October, Kaunda said he had not been brought before a court, that the offence is bailable, that he has a fixed address in Lusaka and is not a flight risk, and that he would provide traceable sureties and not interfere with witnesses. His lawyers argued that an arrested person must be brought before a court within 24 hours or, where that is not practicable, considered for release on bond under section 33 of the Criminal Procedure Code. The Zambian Observer reports that three MPs had stood as sureties for police bond and that he remained in custody even after those conditions were met, which is why he turned to the High Court.

Kaunda is also the respondent in a petition brought by the UPND's candidate in Lima, Lee Mukupa, alleging electoral malpractice; Zambia Monitor gives the August result as 22,760 votes for Kaunda to 8,041 for Mukupa. The petition is being heard at the Lusaka High Court by Judge Derrick Mulenga of the Ndola High Court. The Zambian Observer reported on Tuesday that Kaunda, 43, gave evidence on Monday and denied that there had been widespread violence in the 13 August election, saying there were isolated incidents. He told the court he voted at Ballastone Secondary School, went on to Eden University and later escorted the NRPUP presidential candidate, Brian Mundubile, to vote at Olympia Secondary School, and that Lima's 13 polling stations recorded turnout of about 47.7 per cent with no objections raised after the counts.

A second witness, a 60-year-old supervisor at Eden University who said Kaunda was his employer, described an incident in July in which, he said, a group arriving in UPND-branded vehicles injured three workers at the university's construction site. Under cross-examination he denied that his evidence was motivated by a wish to protect his job. The petition's allegations are the petitioner's case and remain to be decided; the court has given no ruling.

body.confirmed: Kaunda was arrested on 15 October and charged with assault occasioning actual bodily harm (Zambia Monitor; News Diggers). Judge Ndulo set the bail hearing for 27 October (News Diggers). He gave evidence in the Lima petition on Monday (Zambian Observer).
body.unverified: The grant of bail, its terms and the judge's reasons rest on a single report, by the Zambian Observer. The assault allegation is untested: Kaunda has not been tried and no plea has been reported. The petition's allegations of violence are denied and undecided.

stories.title: Four wins, 22 goals and a seven-goal afternoon for Maxen Msimuko: Zambia's under-15s finish second in their group at the first FIFA U-15 World Cup and go into Tier B
stories.excerpt: The Junior Chipolopolo beat Comoros 3–2 on Monday to close Group X with wins over Tanzania, Moldova, Montserrat and Comoros and a single defeat to Uruguay, finishing level on 12 points with the group winners. As runners-up they play on in Tier B of a 189-team, eight-a-side festival in Baku, with round two on Wednesday and the finals on Friday.

image.label: Group X
image.caption: Zambia's under-15 boys won four of five group matches at the inaugural FIFA U-15 World Cup and Festival in Baku, Azerbaijan, in October 2026.

body: Zambia's under-15 boys have finished their group at the inaugural FIFA U-15 World Cup and Festival in Baku with four wins from five matches. News Diggers reports that the Junior Chipolopolo closed their Group X programme with a 3–2 win over Comoros on Monday 26 October, having opened with a 3–1 win over Tanzania on Saturday, lost 3–1 to Uruguay on Sunday, beaten Moldova 2–1 and thrashed Montserrat 13–0. In its account of the Montserrat rout, the paper credits Maxen Msimuko, described as a Young Crocs striker, with seven goals, Simon Nyirenda with two, and Benson Bwalya, Chrispin Katoba, Thomson Mwashilinji and Samuel Musonda with one each.

A COSAFA round-up distributed by AllAfrica on Tuesday gives the group picture. Zambia finished second on 12 points, level with Uruguay, having scored 22 goals. Comoros finished the group on four points. The tournament, which brings together 189 national teams, is played eight-a-side in 40-minute matches, and when the group stage ended on Monday the teams were split into six tiers: the 32 group winners into Tier A, playing for the overall title, and the runners-up into Tier B, playing for positions 33 to 64. Zambia therefore goes into Tier B against other group runners-up; the opponents are decided by a draw and had not been named in either report.

Angola lead the southern African charge. COSAFA reports that they won all five Group J matches, including 4–0 against Saudi Arabia, 3–2 against China and 2–1 against Japan, to top their group with 15 points and go into Tier A. South Africa finished second in Group A on ten points, with a 13–1 win over Anguilla, an 8–0 win over the Maldives and a 3–2 win over France among their results, and Madagascar were second in Group T on 12 points after beating Mozambique 2–0. Mozambique, Malawi and Namibia finished third in their groups; Zimbabwe, Lesotho and Mauritius fourth; Botswana took six points; and Eswatini, Comoros and the Seychelles finished lower. All 14 COSAFA members remain in the competition, since every team is guaranteed further matches.

Round two is on Wednesday 28 October, with more fixtures on Thursday and the six tier finals on Friday 30 October at Baku's Crystal Hall, according to COSAFA. Neither report names Zambia's coach or the squad's next opponents.

stories.title: Chulu and Mbevya win in Monze as MO Drive take a one-two in round three of the national rally championship, with Zain Sidique still leading the standings
stories.excerpt: The Afrivert Energy Monze Motor Rally ran more than 91 km of gravel and plantation stages over the weekend of 24–25 October, backed by a K300,000 sponsorship pool. Geoffrey Chulu and navigator Kapuzya Mbevya won from team-mates Charles Hanankuni and Lweendo Simunzele, with the father-and-son Mukosa crew third. The title is decided at the final round in late November.

image.label: Monze Rally
image.caption: The Afrivert Energy Monze Motor Rally, the third round of the 2026 Zambia National Rally Championship, was run over the weekend of 24–25 October 2026.

body: Geoffrey Chulu and his navigator Kapuzya Mbevya won the Afrivert Energy Monze Motor Rally over the weekend, the third round of the 2026 Zambia National Rally Championship, the Times of Zambia reported on Tuesday 27 October. Driving car number 5 for the MO Drive Racing Team, they finished ahead of team-mates Charles Hanankuni and Lweendo Simunzele in car 26, giving the team a one-two. Third place went to Kenny Mukosa Snr, with his son Kenny Mukosa Jr reading the notes, in car 6 for the Ntengwa Mubili team.

Zain Sidique and Michael Chulu, in car 10 for Pick a Part Racing, were fourth, and Abusahid Patel and Choolwe Chibika finished fifth in car 21 for Cazylinc. Despite finishing off the podium, Sidique still leads the 2026 championship standings, according to the paper, which gives no points totals. The fourth and final round is scheduled for late November, when the national champion will be crowned.

The rally was organised by the Monze Motor Club in partnership with Afrivert Energy, with a corporate sponsorship pool the Times puts at K300,000. It was launched ceremonially at Monze Golf Club and run over more than 91.68 km of stages on gravel tracks and plantation roads around the Southern Province farming town, drawing hundreds of spectators from Monze and further afield. The paper's account singles out the Mukosas' drifting on the loose surfaces and a heavy-duty V8 Land Rover driven by local favourites, whose crew it does not name.

Monze's rally sits in a domestic calendar that has had the lion's share of attention this week going to Red Arrows, whose qualification for the CAF Confederation Cup group stage was covered by Lusaka Brief on Sunday and Monday. The group-stage draw for that competition was scheduled for Wednesday 28 October, according to a list of the 16 qualified clubs published by Africa Soccer on Sunday, which names Red Arrows as Zambia's representative alongside Al Ahly, Raja Casablanca, USM Alger and South Africa's Durban City.

stories.title: 'Ministry on wheels': the President delivers the bus he promised Adventist youth at July's Big Sabbath, and the Lusaka Conference asks its members to keep praying for him
stories.excerpt: Pastor Francis Chibiya, president of the Seventh-day Adventist Church's Lusaka Conference, unveiled the vehicle pledged by President Hichilema on 27 July at the Blessing Centre. The bus will carry Pathfinders to camporees and young people to retreats and evangelistic campaigns; the church did not give its cost or capacity.

image.label: Big Sabbath
image.caption: President Hichilema pledged a bus to the Seventh-day Adventist Lusaka Conference's youth department at the Youth Big Sabbath on 27 July 2026 and has now delivered it.

body: The Seventh-day Adventist Church's Lusaka Conference has taken delivery of a bus pledged by President Hakainde Hichilema three months ago. The Times of Zambia reported on Tuesday 27 October that the President made the promise on 27 July, when he was guest of honour at the Youth Big Sabbath at the Blessing Centre, and that the conference president, Pastor Francis Chibiya, led the unveiling. The President was not present for the handover.

Chibiya said the vehicle was more than transport and would bring renewed excitement and hope to the church's youth and their leaders. "It is ministry on wheels," he said. The bus is to support youth-led initiatives, carry Pathfinders to camporees and take young people to conferences, spiritual retreats, evangelistic campaigns and other church activities; the conference expects it to strengthen youth evangelism and community outreach across its territory. The conference's youth director, David Kayaya, also thanked the President. Both men asked church members to keep praying for the President, government leaders and the nation.

The Times of Zambia's report does not give the make, model, capacity or cost of the bus, the date or venue of the unveiling beyond its being led by Chibiya, or whether the vehicle was given personally by the President or through a public body. No government statement on the gift was reported. The pledge was made at the youth ministries department's Big Sabbath, where the President was guest of honour, and the bus goes to that department rather than to the conference as a whole.

The report records the delivery, the thanks and the prayers, and little else. Whether the bus was a personal gift or came through a public body, and what it cost, are the questions a fuller account would answer; Tuesday's does not, and nothing else read for this edition does either.

analysis.title: Thirty ministries in a day: what Tuesday settled and what it left open
analysis.body: The motion went from announcement to approval in a day, and in the order the Constitution sets out: the structure first, the appointments after. That supplies an explanation for the Cabinet of four that no official had given aloud, which is that ministers were not being named to ministries about to be redrawn. It does not settle the political argument. Nothing published with the motion says what six more ministries will cost, and the documents, by the Zambian Observer's reading, describe how functions will be divided rather than show why dividing them will work better. The strongest case for the government is Sunday Chanda's: that fuel security, housing finance and domestic processing each need an owner with a budget, and that the test is the first 90 days. The strongest case against is Chapter One's and Mushimba's: that structure is cheap to draw and expensive to staff, and that the same results could be bought with a stronger civil service. What to watch: who takes Electricity and Petroleum, whether Mutati and Syakalima go to ministries or stay on the back benches, and whether the budget is read to a full front bench.

analysis.title: The budget nobody has yet defended
analysis.body: Citizens First's objection is procedural, but it is not trivial. A budget is a statement of collective responsibility, and for eleven weeks there has been very little collective to be responsible. If the presentation goes ahead on Friday, ministers appointed this week will be asked in the sector committees to defend allocations negotiated by permanent secretaries and the Ministry of Finance. If it is pushed back, the ten working days of sector analysis and the 24 November resumption move with it, and the Treasury bill auction on Thursday will be read against a budget that has not been seen. ZIPAR's advice not to touch PAYE is the more consequential signal for households: it suggests the institute expects the 2027 numbers to be tight, with the growth agenda needing every kwacha of revenue. The doctors' 15 per cent ask and the agriculture lobby's FISP complaints are claims on the same envelope. What to watch: whether the date holds, whether the Finance Minister reads the speech to a full front bench, and what the Thursday auction says about who will lend to pay for it.

analysis.title: A train is a cholera outbreak with a timetable
analysis.body: Monday's quarantine at Mapepe is the kind of event an outbreak plan is written for, and on the evidence of two reports it was handled quickly: the train was held, the sick were isolated at a treatment centre, and 500 doses of vaccine were brought to the passengers rather than the passengers to the vaccine. The harder questions are upstream. The Permanent Secretary's account has the first case boarding somewhere on the line, with Kapiri Mposhi the place he named; a train that leaves the Copperbelt and crosses Central Province before reaching Lusaka carries the outbreak's geography with it. The national count has also moved faster than the daily headlines suggest, from 1,314 cases to 1,488 between one tally and the next, with 29 deaths. A passenger train is a moving market: hundreds of people, shared water and food, and a day on board. What to watch: whether districts along the route report cases in the coming days, whether Zambia Railways' promised surveillance means screening before boarding rather than after, and whether the ZNPHI reconciles its two running tallies into one figure the public can follow.
